findings.title: Possible covert-channel candidate: http Host header of 192.168.1.69
findings.description: The Host header field across 296 HTTP messages from 192.168.1.69 varies over a small alphabet (, 192.168.48.134:8080) in a two-state repeated sequence. Mapping the values to bits and grouping 8 per byte yields 37 bytes that decode to printable-looking output (100%).
findings.explanation: Protocol metadata fields that the sender can freely choose (HTTP version, query type, TTL, portΓÇª) can carry hidden information by *value selection*: every packet is legal on its own, and only the sequence encodes data. This is an indicator, not proof ΓÇö the same variation can occur naturally (client pools, load balancers). Judge by whether the decoded output is meaningful and whether the pattern persists. Full derivation: `netsleuth covert <pcap>`.
findings.verification: In Wireshark: http.host && ip.src == 192.168.1.69 ΓÇö read the field of each packet in order, note the values (the engine observed: ├ù149, 192.168.48.134:8080├ù147), assign bits per the mapping and decode 8 bits per byte.

findings.title: Possible port scan from 192.168.1.69 (296 connection attempts)
findings.description: 192.168.1.69 sent SYN packets to 1 distinct ports on other hosts; only 0 handshakes completed.
findings.explanation: A SYN scan probes many ports quickly to find open services without completing connections. Legitimate software rarely touches dozens of ports on remote hosts in one burst ΓÇö but load balancers and monitoring systems sometimes do, so check what 192.168.1.69 is before concluding.
findings.verification: In Wireshark, filter for this source's SYN packets ("ip.src == 192.168.1.69 && tcp.flags.syn == 1 && !tcp.flags.ack") and check which ports answered SYN+ACK.

mitre.name: Network Service Discovery
mitre.why: mass TCP SYN probing of many ports

findings.title: Periodic connections: 192.168.1.69 ΓåÆ 10.10.10.10:8080 (296 connections, ~0.0s interval)
findings.description: 192.168.1.69 connected to 10.10.10.10:8080 296 times with a mean interval of 0.0s and low timing variance (CV=0.36).
findings.explanation: Malware check-ins are often timer-driven, so their connection intervals are far more regular than human-driven traffic. BUT: software updaters, NTP clients, monitoring agents and messaging apps also produce regular traffic. This is an indicator to investigate, not evidence of compromise on its own. Check the destination's reputation and the stream content.
findings.verification: In Wireshark: ip.addr == 10.10.10.10 && tcp.port == 8080 ΓÇö look at the time column (╬ötime) between connections.
evidence: payload size uniformity: CV 0.35 across 296 data-bearing connections

mitre.why: regularly-timed repeated connections consistent with a C2 check-in schedule

findings.title: Uncommon HTTP methods used: DELETE, PATCH, PUT
findings.description: 192 request(s) used methods outside the usual GET/POST set.
findings.explanation: TRACE can reflect credentials (XST), CONNECT proxies tunnels, and PUT/DELETE on unexpected endpoints often means someone is probing an API or trying to plant content. REST APIs use these methods legitimately ΓÇö context decides.
findings.verification: In Wireshark: http.request.method in {DELETE PATCH PUT}
